chapter_seo_title: Dao Gui Yi Xian Ch. 601 – Li Huowang Bites His Way Out of Hypnosis
chapter_meta_description: Forced to take drugs to prove his “powers,” Li Huowang regresses into the Dao-Twisted World—only to vomit the pills out and attack Wu Cheng with a saw and his own teeth.
og_title: DGYX 601: The Pills—Li Huowang Refuses to Be a Lab Rat
og_description: A dying old man wants proof of magic. A psychologist wants a docile subject. Li Huowang wants flesh in his mouth.
twitter_title: When “just say yes” becomes a bite in the face—Li Huowang Ch. 601
twitter_description: Drug-induced regression to the Dao-Twisted World, a fatal conversation with Huangfu Tiangang, and Li Huowang vomiting pills to bite his tormentor.

lore_anchors.definition: Pills that extend one’s lifespan, derived from the essence of Heart-Element alchemy. In this novel, they are a rare commodity traded by the powerful and craved by the dying.
A fictional sect blending elements of Zoroastrianism and Nestorian Christianity, centering on a “Gu-Spirit” and suffering as a path to power.
The deity worshiped by the Ao-Jing Sect, often depicted on a twisted cross—a symbol of pain, sacrifice, and esoteric exchange.
The Da Liang Imperial Preceptor, a powerful practitioner of lightning-based techniques and a figure whose loyalties are deeply suspect.
A geomantic energy channel in Chinese cosmology that determines a dynasty’s fate; in this novel, it is a tangible, vulnerable attachment on the Emperor’s spine.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does Li Huowang bite Wu Cheng?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Because vomiting out the drug slurry and attacking with his teeth is the only weapon he has left. Every other limb is restrained; his body itself becomes a tool of defiance.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Is this the real Huangfu Tiangang?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The chapter deliberately blurs the line. Under hypnosis and drugs, Li Huowang’s perception is unreliable—but the novel has already established that Huangfu Tiangang truly exists in the Dao-Twisted World and has his own agenda.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What is the significance of the "finger-saw"?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Self-mutilation is a recurring method Li Huowang uses to regain control when his mind or body is being manipulated. The saw is both a physical tool and a psychic anchor—pain breaks the spell.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Can drugs really trigger xianxia hallucinations?
cultural_notes_faq.a: In the novel’s framework, the medication doesn't create the hallucinations; it suppresses Li Huowang’s learned coping mechanisms, allowing the "realer" Dao-Twisted World perceptions to surface.
